newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Chronology of key EU treaties.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of key EU treaties.

text.p: Following are the key treaties that created what is now known as the European Union:
-- April 1951: The treaty to create a European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) is signed in Paris.
Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany agree to place their coal and steel industries under a common authority.
-- March 1957: The six countries sign treaties to create the European Economic Community (EEC) and the European Atomic Energy Community (Euratom).

The EEC Treaty, or Treaty of Rome, aims to eliminate tariffs, quotas and other trade barriers between the member countries and to guarantee that persons, services and capital can move freely across borders. It establishes common policies in areas including agriculture, external trade, competition policy and transport.
The Euratom treaty aims to promote the use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes.
-- April 1965: The six countries sign a treaty to merge the executive institutions of the ECSC, EEC and Euratom, creating the European Community.
-- December 1985: The EC countries -- now including Britain, Denmark, Greece and Ireland -- adopt the Single European Act.

It amends the EC treaties to speed up decision-making to facilitate the effort to create a true border-free market, expanding the use of majority voting. Spain and Portugal join the EC the following month.
-- February 1992: The EC countries sign the Maastricht Treaty creating the European Union.
It calls for creation of a single currency by 1999 and development of a common foreign and security policy, while giving the European Parliament veto power over some legislation.
-- March 1996: The EU countries -- now including Austria, Finland and Sweden -- launch an inter-governmental conference to review the Maastricht Treaty.

It is expected to present draft treaty revisions to EU leaders at a summit in Amsterdam in June, covering areas such as decision-making procedures as the EU grows to take in new members from eastern and central Europe.
